q: After preparing the trial balance the accountant finds that the total of debit side is short by Rs.3,000. The difference will be

options.C: Adjusted to any of the debit balance account
options.D: Adjusted to any of the credit balance.

e: The correct option is (B) Debited to suspense account: when the debit side of the trial balance is short, the shortfall is debited to the Suspense Account to make the totals agree temporarily. q: Recording of outstanding salary is based on
e: The correct option is (A) Accrual concept: outstanding salary is recorded because expenses are recognised when incurred, not when paid — the essence of the accrual (mercantile) concept. Outstanding expenses are incurred but unpaid at year-end; they are provided for so the year's true cost is captured. Remember: Watch the timeline or sequence in such questions; many errors come from mixing up the order.

q: Classify the money spent of Rs.1,00,000 as travelling expenses of the Member Mechanical on trips abroad for purchase of capital asset is
e: The correct option is (A) Capital expenditure: travelling expenses incurred for purchasing a capital asset form part of the asset's cost and are therefore capitalised. Any cost necessary to bring the asset to its intended use is capital expenditure. Capital expenditure creates or improves a durable asset (or reduces a liability); it is not consumed within the year, unlike revenue expenditure. Remember: Note the exact terminology used — the exam rewards precise vocabulary.

q: A Suspense Account balance is
e: The correct option is (C) Debit or credit: a suspense account balance can be either debit or credit, depending on which side of the trial balance was short. If the debit side is short, it shows a debit balance, and vice versa. The trial balance lists all ledger balances to check arithmetical accuracy — total debits must equal total credits. Remember: Practice restating the logic in your own words — recall beats recognition in the exam hall.

q: Closing, Rectification and Adjustment entries are made in which subsidiary Book.
e: The correct option is (C) Journal Proper: closing, rectification and adjustment entries are recorded in the Journal Proper, since they do not fit any special subsidiary book like the cash book or purchases book. The journal is the book of original entry where transactions are first recorded chronologically with debit and credit. Remember: Practice restating the logic in your own words — recall beats recognition in the exam hall.

q: Which of the following statements is correct?
e: Option A (Goodwill is a fictitious asset) is the correct choice. The correct option is (A) Goodwill is a fictitious asset: of the given statements, this is the correct one — goodwill is an intangible/fictitious asset appearing in the books. Patents are intangible (not tangible), debtors are current assets (not liabilities), and land is a fixed asset (not current). Exam note: fictitious assets are expenses/losses not yet written off, like preliminary expenses.

q: Identified & Measured economic events should be recorded in
e: The correct answer is Chronological order. The correct option is (A) Chronological order: identified and measured economic events are recorded in the journal in the order in which they occur. This date-wise recording is the very basis of the journal as the book of original entry. Exam note: the journal is called the book of original (prime) entry; posting to the ledger follows. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.

q: The payment of a Promissory Note is made by its
e: The correct option is (A) Maker: the payment of a promissory note is made by its maker — the person who promises to pay the stated sum. q: Which of the following is not depreciated
e: Land is not depreciated because it normally has an unlimited useful life and does not wear out. Plant and machinery, vehicles and furniture have limited useful lives and are depreciated.

q: Rule of thumb for acid-test ratio is
e: The correct option is (C) 1:1: the rule of thumb for the acid-test (quick) ratio is 1:1, meaning liquid assets should at least equal current liabilities. Liquid assets exclude stock and prepaid expenses from current assets. Prepaid expenses are paid in advance for a future period; they appear as an asset (not current year's expense) in the balance sheet. Remember: Practice restating the logic in your own words — recall beats recognition in the exam hall.

q: All of the following are the functions of Management Accounting except
e: The correct option is (D) Ledger posting: ledger posting is a function of financial accounting, not of management accounting. Management accounting is concerned with decision making, measurement and forecasting for internal use. The ledger groups journal entries account-wise, giving the balance of each account for the trial balance and final accounts. q: Which of the Following is true?

options.A: Payback period method measures the true profitability of a project
options.B: Internal rate of return and time adjusted rate of return are the same
options.C: Capital rationing and capital budgeting mean the same thing
options.D: Average Rate of return method takes into account the time value of money

e: Option B (Internal rate of return and time adjusted rate of return are the same) is the correct choice. The correct option is (B): the internal rate of return and the time-adjusted rate of return are the same thing — the discount rate at which the net present value of a project becomes zero. Both are discounted cash flow techniques of capital budgeting. Exam note: the payback period, which ignores the time value of money, is a traditional (non-discounted) method.

q: Fiscal Means?
e: The correct option is (B) Government Budget: 'fiscal' relates to government revenue and expenditure, so 'fiscal' means the government's budget and its finances. The key is the precise meaning the question tests: each option describes a closely related but distinct idea, and only one fits the definition exactly. q: Agreements that do not give rise to contractual obligations are not contracts.

options.C: Required to the extent of consideration

e: True: an agreement that does not give rise to contractual obligations is not a contract — under Section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act, only an agreement enforceable by law is a contract. Social or moral promises made without intention to create legal relations are not contracts.

q: Recognition of expenses in the same period as associated revenues is known as the
e: The correct option is (B) matching principle: recognising expenses in the same period as the revenues they helped earn is the matching concept. It ensures profit for a period is measured correctly by pairing costs with related revenues. Prepaid expenses are paid in advance for a future period; they appear as an asset (not current year's expense) in the balance sheet. q: If a concern proposes to discontinue its business from March 2018 and decides to dispose of all its assets within a period of 4 months, The Balance Sheet as on

options.D: Cost price or Market value, whichever is lower.

e: The correct answer is Net realisable value. The correct option is (B) Net realisable value: when a business is discontinuing and will dispose of its assets, the going-concern assumption fails, so the balance sheet is prepared at net realisable (liquidation) value rather than historical cost. Assets are stated at what they can actually fetch on sale. Exam note: the going-concern concept is one of the fundamental accounting assumptions; its absence changes the valuation basis.

q: A concept that a business enterprise will not be sold or liquidated in the near future is known as:
e: The correct option is (A) Going Concern: the concept that a business will continue operating in the foreseeable future — not be sold or liquidated — is the going-concern assumption. It justifies recording assets at cost and spreading costs over useful lives. Audit is the independent examination of accounts to verify their truth, fairness and compliance with rules and sanctions. Remember: Note the exact terminology used — the exam rewards precise vocabulary.

q: During the life-time of an entity accounting produce financial statements in accordance with which basic accounting concept:
e: The correct answer is Accounting Period. The correct option is (C) Accounting Period: financial statements are produced at regular intervals during an entity's life in accordance with the accounting period concept. It divides the continuous life of the business into periods like a year or quarter. Exam note: in India the accounting (financial) year for most purposes runs from 1 April to 31 March. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.

q: The concept which requires that the same accounting method should be used from one accounting period to the next is called
e: Consistency — that is the right answer. A change in method is permitted only for a justified reason and must be disclosed. Exam note: consistency is one of the three fundamental accounting assumptions recognised in India. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.

q: All of the following items are classified as fundamental accounting assumptions except
e: The correct option is (B) Business Entity: the fundamental accounting assumptions are going concern, consistency and accrual — the business entity (separate entity) concept is a basic concept but is classified separately from these three assumptions. q: Nandini enterprises follows the Written Down Value method of depreciating machinery year after year due to
e: The correct option is (C) Consistency: Nandini Enterprises uses the Written Down Value method year after year in line with the consistency concept, which demands the same depreciation method across periods for comparability. q: Mr. Raj purchased goods costing 1,50,000 and sold 4/5th of the goods amounting to Rs.1,80,000. He met expenses amounting to Rs.25,000 during the year, 2018. He made a net profit as Rs.35,000. Which of the accounting concept was followed by him?
e: Matching — that is the right answer. The correct option is (C) Matching: Mr. Raj matched the cost of goods sold (4/5 of purchases) and the year's expenses against the year's sales to arrive at net profit — the matching concept in action. Only the cost of goods actually sold is charged against revenue. Exam note: unsold stock (1/5 of goods) stays in the balance sheet as closing stock. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.

q: ‘For each and Every Debit there must be a corresponding Credit’ is the principal of____
e: The correct answer is Double Entry. The correct option is (D) Double Entry: 'for every debit there must be a corresponding credit' is the cardinal principle of the double-entry system of book-keeping. Every transaction affects at least two accounts with equal debit and credit. Exam note: the double-entry system was popularised by Luca Pacioli in 1494. The principle behind this is worth grasping, not just memorising: once you understand why the rule is framed this way, the answer follows naturally instead of needing rote recall.

q: The balance of the petty cash is
e: The correct option is (C) An asset: the balance of petty cash is cash in hand with the petty cashier, hence a current asset of the business. q: A trial balance will not balance if

options.A: Correct Journal entry is posted twice
options.B: The purchase on credit basis is debited to purchases and credited to cash
options.C: Rs.1,000 cash payment to creditors is debited to creditors for Rs.100 and credited to cash Rs.1,000.

e: Option C (Rs.1,000 cash payment to creditors is debited to creditors for Rs.100 and credited to cash Rs.1,000.) is the correct choice. The correct option is (C): when a ₹1,000 cash payment to creditors is debited to creditors for only ₹100 but credited to cash for ₹1,000, the two sides differ and the trial balance will not balance. An error of unequal debit and credit in one entry breaks the agreement of the trial balance. Exam note: errors like posting the correct entry twice do not affect the trial balance's agreement.

q: After the preparation of ledgers , the next step is preparation of
e: Option B (Trial Balance) is the correct choice. q: Rs.20,000 paid as wages for erecting a machine should debited to
e: The correct answer is Machine account. The correct option is (C) Machine account: wages paid for erecting a machine are part of the cost of bringing the machine into working condition, so they are capitalised by debiting the Machine Account. Such installation costs add to the asset's value. Exam note: only revenue-type repairs go to a repairs account; installation is capital. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded. q: Sales of office furniture should be credited to
e: The correct answer is Furniture Account. The correct option is (B) Furniture Account: sale of office furniture — a fixed asset — is credited to the Furniture Account, not to the Sales Account, because sales account records only sale of goods dealt in. This distinguishes asset disposal from trading revenue. Exam note: any profit or loss on such sale is transferred to the profit and loss account. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded. q: Rent paid to landlord is credited to
e: The correct answer is Cash a/c. The correct option is (C) Cash a/c: rent paid to the landlord is credited to the Cash Account because cash goes out of the business — the landlord's account is debited and cash is credited. The payment reduces the cash balance. Exam note: in double entry, every payment entry credits cash (or bank) and debits the expense or the person paid. The principle behind this is worth grasping, not just memorising: once you understand why the rule is framed this way, the answer follows naturally instead of needing rote recall.

q: If the assets of a business are Rs.3,00,000 and its capital Rs.1,00,000, the liabilities of this business are
e: The correct option is (B) 2,00,000: by the accounting equation, Liabilities = Assets − Capital = ₹3,00,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹2,00,000. Capital is the owner's claim, and liabilities are outsiders' claims on the assets. q: Effect of machinery purchased for cash

options.C: No change in the total assets.

e: Option C (No change in the total assets.) is the correct choice. The correct option is (C) No change in the total assets: buying machinery for cash merely converts one asset (cash) into another (machinery) of equal value, so total assets stay the same. The accounting equation remains balanced with no change in liabilities either. Exam note: such exchanges are called asset-for-asset transactions. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.

q: Recording of outstanding salary is based on
e: The correct option is (A) Accrual concept: outstanding salary is recognised on the accrual basis — expenses are recorded when the obligation arises (service rendered), irrespective of payment. This is why unpaid salaries appear as a liability at year-end. Outstanding expenses are incurred but unpaid at year-end; they are provided for so the year's true cost is captured. q: Goodwill Account is a
e: Real Account — that is the right answer. Real accounts follow the rule: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Exam note: personal accounts relate to persons, nominal accounts to expenses, incomes, gains and losses. q: A withdrawal of goods from business by the proprietor should be credited to which Account.

q: What checks the arithmetical accuracy of ledger accounts?

q: The process of transferring debit and credit items from a journal to their respective Accounts in the ledger is termed as
e: Option A (Ledger Posting) is the correct choice. q: Cash book is journal as well as
e: The correct option is (B) Ledger: the cash book is both a journal (book of original entry for cash transactions) and a ledger, because the cash and bank columns serve as the Cash Account and Bank Account — no separate posting is needed. q: Contingent Asset usually arises from unplanned or unexpected events that give rise to:

options.A: The possibility of an inflow of economic benefits to the business entity
options.B: The possibility of an outflow of economic benefits to the business entity

e: Option A (The possibility of an inflow of economic benefits to the business entity) is the correct choice. q: Balance of indirect expenses accounts are transferred to
e: The correct answer is Profit & Loss account. q: The capital of a sole trader would change as a result of

q: A decrease in the provision for doubtful debts would result in:
e: Option D (An increase in Net profits) is the correct choice. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded. The paper tests exact scope here, not an approximate idea, which is why careful reading of the question stem matters.

q: The Debts written off as bad, if recovered subsequently are

options.A: Credited to Bad Debts recovered account
options.C: Debited to Profit and Loss Account

e: The correct option is (A) Credited to Bad Debts recovered account: bad debts written off earlier, if recovered later, are treated as a gain and credited to the 'Bad Debts Recovered' account. The debtor's account is not reopened. The trading and profit & loss account arrives at gross and net results by matching revenues with the costs of the period. Remember: Remember the underlying principle, not just the sentence: examiners often rephrase the same concept.

q: Provision for Bad and Doubtful Debts is treated in the balance sheet as
e: The correct option is (D) Deducted from Debtors: the provision for bad and doubtful debts is shown in the balance sheet as a deduction from sundry debtors, presenting debtors at their estimated realisable value. It is a contra-asset, not a liability. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and capital at a point of time — what the entity owns and owes. Remember: Watch the timeline or sequence in such questions; many errors come from mixing up the order.

q: Identified and measured economic events should be recorded in
e: The correct option is (A) chronological order: identified and measured economic events are recorded date-wise in the books — the journal captures transactions in the sequence they happen. Chronological recording preserves the audit trail. The journal is the book of original entry where transactions are first recorded chronologically with debit and credit. Remember: Practice restating the logic in your own words — recall beats recognition in the exam hall.

q: A Suspense Account balance is
e: Debit or credit — that is the right answer. The correct option is (C) Debit or credit: a suspense account may show either a debit or a credit balance — it depends on which side of the trial balance fell short. The balance simply equals the difference needing investigation. Exam note: a suspense account never appears in the final published balance sheet once errors are rectified. The principle behind this is worth grasping, not just memorising: once you understand why the rule is framed this way, the answer follows naturally instead of needing rote recall.

q: When a debtor pays her dues

options.A: Assets side of Balance sheet will increase
options.B: Assets side of Balance Sheet will decrease
options.C: Liabilities side of Balance Sheet will increase
options.D: There will be no change in total assets or total liabilities

e: There will be no change in total assets or total liabilities — that is the right answer. The correct option is (D): when a debtor pays, one asset (debtors) decreases and another (cash) increases by the same amount, so there is no change in total assets or total liabilities. It is a pure asset-exchange transaction. Exam note: only transactions with outsiders involving income, expense, capital or liabilities change the totals. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded.

q: Claim admitted in respect of stock destroyed by fire will be credited to
e: Option B (Purchases Account) is the correct choice. The correct option is (B) Purchases Account: a claim admitted by the insurer for stock destroyed by fire is credited to the Purchases Account, because the destroyed stock was originally debited there — the claim offsets the loss of goods. The corresponding debit goes to the insurance company (a debtor). Exam note: any shortfall between claim and stock value is debited to the profit and loss account as loss by fire.

q: Patents, Copyrights and Trademarks are
e: The correct answer is Intangible assets. The correct option is (C) Intangible assets: patents, copyrights and trademarks are intangible assets — identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance, held for long-term use. They appear under fixed (non-current) assets but lack physical form. Exam note: goodwill is also intangible, but it is often classed as a fictitious asset in older texts. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded. The paper tests exact scope here, not an approximate idea, which is why careful reading of the question stem matters.

q: Balance sheets are prepared
e: The correct option is (D) Annually: balance sheets are prepared annually at the end of the accounting year to present the financial position on that date. Final accounts are yearly statements by convention and law. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and capital at a point of time — what the entity owns and owes. Remember: Note the exact terminology used — the exam rewards precise vocabulary.

q: Book-Keeping is mainly concerned with

options.B: Designing the systems of classifying and summarising the recorded data.
options.C: Interpreting the data for internal and external users.

e: recording of financial data. — that is the right answer. The correct option is (A) recording of financial data: book-keeping is mainly concerned with the systematic recording of financial transactions — journalising and posting. Classifying, summarising and interpreting are the wider functions of accounting. Exam note: book-keeping is the recording phase; accounting adds analysis and interpretation. The principle behind this is worth grasping, not just memorising: once you understand why the rule is framed this way, the answer follows naturally instead of needing rote recall.

q: Preparation of a Trial balance is for:
e: Option C (The trial balance to agree.) is the correct choice. The correct option is (C): preparation of a trial balance is for making the trial balance agree — its primary purpose is to verify the arithmetical accuracy of the books. Locating errors is a by-product when it fails to agree. Exam note: agreement of the trial balance is a test of arithmetical accuracy, not a proof of complete correctness. The principle behind this is worth grasping, not just memorising: once you understand why the rule is framed this way, the answer follows naturally instead of needing rote recall.

q: Cash Book which is maintained to record small expenses is called.
e: petty cash book. — that is the right answer. The correct option is (B) petty cash book: the cash book maintained to record small day-to-day expenses is called the petty cash book, usually operated by a petty cashier on the imprest system. It keeps minor payments separate from the main cash book. Exam note: under the imprest system, the petty cashier is reimbursed periodically to restore a fixed float. This provision exists for a practical reason in day-to-day railway working; keeping that practical picture in mind makes the fact far easier to retain than memorising it in isolation.

q: What is that maintained for known liabilities
e: The correct option is (A) Provision: a provision is maintained for known liabilities of uncertain amount or timing — e.g. provision for taxation or for doubtful debts. It is a charge against profit, not an appropriation. Appropriation is Parliament's authorisation, through the Appropriation Act, to withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund for the voted demands. Remember: Practice restating the logic in your own words — recall beats recognition in the exam hall.

q: Closing, Rectification and Adjustment entries are made in which subsidiary Book.
e: Option C (Journal Proper) is the correct choice. The correct option is (C) Journal Proper: closing, rectification and adjustment entries are recorded in the Journal Proper, as they belong to no special subsidiary book. The journal proper is the residuary book for all such entries. Exam note: adjustment entries (outstanding, prepaid, depreciation) are passed at the end of the accounting period. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.

q: Journal Proper records

options.C: All transactions not recorded in any subsidiary books

e: All transactions not recorded in any subsidiary books — that is the right answer. The correct option is (C): the Journal Proper records all transactions not recorded in any subsidiary books — it is the residuary journal for opening, closing, adjustment, rectification and transfer entries. Special journals handle repetitive transactions. Exam note: credit purchases and credit sales go to their own subsidiary books, not the journal proper.

q: Real Account records
e: The correct answer is Dealings in commodities. The correct option is (B): a Real Account records dealings in commodities and properties — i.e. assets of the business, such as machinery, stock and cash. Real accounts carry the rule 'debit what comes in, credit what goes out'. Exam note: real accounts are not closed at year-end; their balances are carried forward. The principle behind this is worth grasping, not just memorising: once you understand why the rule is framed this way, the answer follows naturally instead of needing rote recall.

q: The following is a statement showing the financial status of the company at any given time
e: The correct answer is Balance sheet. The correct option is (C) Balance sheet: the balance sheet is the statement showing the financial status (position) of the company at a given point of time — its assets, liabilities and capital. It is a position statement, not a period statement. Exam note: the trading and profit & loss account, by contrast, covers a period. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.

q: After sale of goods worth Rs.20,000 on March31,2020, a proprietor is left with closing stock of Rs. 10,000. This is

options.C: A transaction as well as event

e: The correct answer is An event. The correct option is (A) An event: closing stock of ₹10,000 after the year's sales is an event (a year-end position), not a transaction, because no exchange with an outside party occurred — it is the result of past transactions. Events affect the accounts without a two-party exchange. Exam note: transactions always involve an exchange; events like stock-taking do not. This provision exists for a practical reason in day-to-day railway working; keeping that practical picture in mind makes the fact far easier to retain than memorising it in isolation.

q: Assets are held in business for the purpose of
e: The correct answer is Earning revenue. The correct option is (C) Earning revenue: assets are held in a business for the purpose of earning revenue — directly (stock sold) or indirectly (machinery used in production). This is the economic rationale for acquiring and retaining assets. Exam note: even cash is held to support revenue-earning operations. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded. The paper tests exact scope here, not an approximate idea, which is why careful reading of the question stem matters.

q: General Reserve is treated in Balance sheet as

options.D: Both as an Asset and a Liability.

e: The correct option is (B) Liability: the General Reserve is treated as a liability in the balance sheet — it is shown under Reserves and Surplus on the liabilities side, since it represents profits retained for the owners. Appropriation is Parliament's authorisation, through the Appropriation Act, to withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund for the voted demands. Remember: Remember the underlying principle, not just the sentence: examiners often rephrase the same concept.

q: Identified & Measured economic events should be recorded in
e: Option A (Chronological order) is the correct choice. The correct option is (A) Chronological order: identified and measured economic events must be recorded in chronological (date-wise) order in the books of original entry. This sequence keeps the records systematic and traceable. Exam note: narration with each journal entry explains the transaction briefly. This provision exists for a practical reason in day-to-day railway working; keeping that practical picture in mind makes the fact far easier to retain than memorising it in isolation.

q: A Suspense Accounts shows this balance
e: The correct option is (C) Debit or credit: a suspense account shows either a debit or a credit balance, depending on which side of the trial balance was short. It simply carries the unlocated difference. The trial balance lists all ledger balances to check arithmetical accuracy — total debits must equal total credits. Remember: Watch the timeline or sequence in such questions; many errors come from mixing up the order.

q: A Profit on the disposal of a fixed asset can also be described as an

options.A: Over provision for depreciation on the asset
options.B: Increase in Fixed Assets on the Balance Sheet
options.C: Under provision for depreciation on the asset

e: Option A (Over provision for depreciation on the asset) is the correct choice. The correct option is (A): a profit on disposal of a fixed asset can be described as an over-provision for depreciation on the asset — the asset was depreciated more than its actual fall in value, so sale proceeds exceed the written-down value. It is a capital profit credited to the profit and loss account. Exam note: such profit arises when accumulated depreciation was excessive relative to actual wear.

q: Capital is the difference between

options.B: Sales and cost of goods sold

e: The correct option is (C) Assets and Liabilities: capital is the difference between assets and liabilities — the owner's residual claim on the business (Assets − Liabilities = Capital). This is a concept-clarity question. The right option follows directly from the definition; the wrong ones look plausible only with an approximate recall. Tighten the definition in your revision notes. Remember: Eliminate the distractors first — each wrong option usually describes a related but different concept.

q: Disagreement of a trial balance indicates the following error
e: Disagreement of the trial balance indicates a one-sided error — an error affecting only one side of a transaction, such as a partial posting or a wrong amount entered on one side only. Errors of omission, duplication, commission and principle affect both sides equally and do not disturb the agreement of the trial balance.

q: Which of the following Statements is false

options.A: Assets will be equal to capital, if there are no liabilities
options.B: Basic Concepts bring uniformity in Accounting
options.D: According to business entity concept the existence of business and proprietors is one and the same.

e: The correct option is (D): the false statement is that 'according to the business entity concept the existence of business and proprietor is one and the same' — the entity concept actually treats them as separate and distinct. An audit para is a formal audit observation; paras are settled through compliance, recovery or regularisation. Remember: Practice restating the logic in your own words — recall beats recognition in the exam hall.

q: What is a Bills Receivable account?
e: The correct option is (C) Real Account: the Bills Receivable account is a real account because a bill receivable is an asset — a document representing money to be received. Real accounts record assets and follow 'debit what comes in'. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and capital at a point of time — what the entity owns and owes. Remember: Remember the underlying principle, not just the sentence: examiners often rephrase the same concept.

q: From the following information, find out who can draw the bill if Mr. A sold goods to B:

options.A: A will draw a bill on B
options.C: Third party will draw a bill on A or B

e: The correct option is (A) A will draw a bill on B: when A sells goods to B on credit, A (the creditor/seller) draws the bill of exchange on B (the debtor/buyer), who accepts it. The drawer is the person entitled to receive the money. The key is the precise meaning the question tests: each option describes a closely related but distinct idea, and only one fits the definition exactly. In the exam, such questions reward careful reading of definitions — compare every option against the textbook meaning word by word.

q: Who draws a Bill of Exchange?
e: The correct answer is Holder. The correct option is (C) Holder: as per the answer key, a bill of exchange is drawn by the holder — the creditor who is entitled to receive payment draws the bill on the debtor, and often retains (holds) it till maturity. In the standard three-party structure the drawer, who draws the bill, is typically the creditor/holder of the claim. Exam note: the three parties to a bill are drawer, drawee and payee.

q: The person who draws a Bill of Exchange is known as
e: The correct option is (A) Drawer: the person who draws (writes) a bill of exchange is known as the drawer — usually the seller/creditor who orders the drawee to pay. The drawer signs the instrument to make it effective. Approach by elimination: strike out the options that contradict the basic principle, and the survivor is your answer. Building this elimination habit speeds up the paper considerably.

q: What does ‘retiring a bill under rebate’ mean?

options.A: Making a payment of the bill before the due date
options.C: Making a payment of the bill after the due date

e: The correct option is (A): 'retiring a bill under rebate' means the drawee pays the bill before its due date and gets a rebate (discount) from the holder for early payment. The rebate is the consideration for paying early. Focus on the exact wording of the question stem: the correct option aligns with the standard definition, while the distractors twist one detail. Training your eye for that one differing word is high-value preparation.

q: A bill of Exchange has __Parties
e: The correct answer is Three. The correct option is (C) Three: a bill of exchange has three parties — the drawer (who draws it), the drawee (on whom it is drawn), and the payee (to whom payment is to be made). All three roles must exist for the instrument to operate. Exam note: a promissory note has only two parties — maker and payee. This provision exists for a practical reason in day-to-day railway working; keeping that practical picture in mind makes the fact far easier to retain than memorising it in isolation.

q: Noting Charges are paid to the Notary by the

options.D: Either of the above three parties

e: The correct option is (D) Either of the above three parties: noting charges — the notary's fee for recording dishonour — are initially paid by the holder but are ultimately recoverable from any of the liable parties (drawer, endorser, or the party at fault), h. The key is the precise meaning the question tests: each option describes a closely related but distinct idea, and only one fits the definition exactly. In the exam, such questions reward careful reading of definitions — compare every option against the textbook meaning word by word.

q: The payment of a Promissory Note is made by its
e: Maker — that is the right answer. The correct option is (A) Maker: the payment of a promissory note is made by its maker, who promised to pay the sum stated in the note. The maker is the debtor party to the instrument. Exam note: unlike a bill of exchange, a promissory note needs no acceptance — the maker's promise itself is the obligation. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.

q: The purpose of accommodation bill is

options.A: To finance actual purchase or sale of goods
options.C: When both parties are in need of funds

e: The correct option is (C): the purpose of an accommodation bill is to help when both parties are in need of funds — it is drawn not for a genuine trade transaction but to raise finance by discounting. Focus on the exact wording of the question stem: the correct option aligns with the standard definition, while the distractors twist one detail. Training your eye for that one differing word is high-value preparation.

q: Under which circumstances drawer and payee is same person:

options.A: When drawer discounted the bill with banker
options.B: When drawer endorse the bill to third party
options.C: When drawer held the bill till maturity
options.D: When drawee rejects to accept the bill

e: The correct option is (C): drawer and payee are the same person when the drawer holds the bill till maturity — the drawer draws the bill on the drawee and retains the right to receive payment himself instead of endorsing it away. This is a concept-clarity question. The right option follows directly from the definition; the wrong ones look plausible only with an approximate recall. Tighten the definition in your revision notes.

q: Debit balance in the Pass Book means:

options.A: Favourable balance in the Cash Book
options.B: Unfavourable balance in the Cash Book
options.C: Favourable balance in the Pass Book
options.D: Unfavourable balance in the Pass Book.

e: The correct option is (D) Unfavourable balance in the Pass Book: a debit balance in the pass book means the bank owes the customer nothing — instead the customer has overdrawn, so it is an unfavourable (overdraft) balance from the customer's view. The key is the precise meaning the question tests: each option describes a closely related but distinct idea, and only one fits the definition exactly. In the exam, such questions reward careful reading of definitions — compare every option against the textbook meaning word by word.

q: Bank Reconciliation Statement is a
e: The correct option is (D) None of the above: the Bank Reconciliation Statement is not a part of the cash book, bank account or financial statements — it is a separate statement (memorandum) prepared to reconcile the cash book and pass book balances. The bank reconciliation statement reconciles the cash book with the bank pass book, explaining timing differences like unpresented cheques. Remember: Make a one-line note of this concept for revision; it recurs in several papers.

q: When balance as per Pass Book is the starting point, interest allowed by bank is
e: The correct option is (B) Subtracted: when the pass book balance is the starting point, interest allowed by the bank has already increased the pass book balance, so to arrive at the cash book balance it must be subtracted. Focus on the exact wording of the question stem: the correct option aligns with the standard definition, while the distractors twist one detail. Training your eye for that one differing word is high-value preparation.
